articles.headline: Treasury Designates Entities in Iran-Related Sanctions Push
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. This action is part of a broader effort to target entities and individuals supporting the Iranian regime.

These designations aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund illicit activities. The specifics of the entities and individuals designated were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but are part of ongoing pressure campaigns.
This move follows a series of similar actions by OFAC throughout the year, underscoring the U.S. government's commitment to its sanctions policy against Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba on November 20, 2026. This dual action highlights OFAC's continued focus on both Iranian and Cuban sanctions programs.

The Iran designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. These actions often target individuals and entities involved in proliferation, terrorism, or human rights abuses.

The issuance of new Cuba FAQs aims to provide clarity and guidance to the public regarding existing sanctions and authorized transactions concerning the island nation. This is a common practice by OFAC to ensure compliance and understanding of complex regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia-Related GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License and an amended Russia-related General License with accompanying Frequently Asked Questions.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting transnational criminal organizations and malicious cyber actors that pose a threat to national security. The Illicit Drugs General License aims to facilitate certain humanitarian or legitimate transactions that might otherwise be prohibited.

The amended Russia-related General License and FAQs provide updated guidance for transactions involving Russia, reflecting the evolving landscape of sanctions in response to ongoing geopolitical developments. This ensures that U.S. persons and entities have the most current information for compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt the financing and support networks of terrorist organizations worldwide.

The designations target individuals and entities found to be providing material support, financial services, or other forms of assistance to designated terrorist groups. Such actions aim to isolate these actors from the international financial system.

These measures reinforce the U.S. commitment to combating terrorism and protecting its national security interests by preventing funds and resources from reaching those who seek to harm innocent civilians.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Narcotics and Terrorism Facilitators
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action reflects the interconnected nature of these illicit networks.

These designations aim to sever financial and logistical support for criminal organizations engaged in drug trafficking and terrorist financing. By targeting these facilitators, OFAC seeks to disrupt their operations and limit their ability to generate and move illicit funds.

The U.S. government continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat threats posed by narcotics traffickers and terrorist groups, safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to its Iran designations on November 9, 2026. This action typically involves modifications to existing listings, such as changes in identifying information or aliases for designated individuals or entities.

Such updates are crucial for maintaining the accuracy and effectiveness of OFAC's sanctions lists, ensuring that financial institutions and other regulated entities can properly identify and block sanctioned parties.
While not a new designation, these updates are an important part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to enforce its comprehensive sanctions regime against Iran.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, as part of its ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' to sever the financial lifelines of the Iranian regime.

These designations target financial networks that are deemed to be sustaining the Iranian regime, aiming to disrupt their ability to generate revenue and fund illicit activities. This action is consistent with the U.S. strategy to increase economic pressure on Iran.
The U.S. government continues to work with international partners to identify and target individuals and entities that facilitate Iran's sanctions evasion and support its destabilizing activities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Criminal Organizations, Adds Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. Additionally, OFAC imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination.

The cyber-related and transnational criminal organization designations aim to disrupt illicit activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic stability. These actions often target ransomware groups, illicit cryptocurrency mixers, and other criminal networks.

The Cuba designations and determination expand the scope of U.S. sanctions against the Cuban economy, specifically extending Executive Order 14404 to four new sectors: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / World Socialist Web Site

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert on November 4, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities and its support for terrorism. The OFAC Alert aims to inform the public about potential risks associated with certain transactions involving Iran.

The amended Venezuela-related General License and FAQ provide updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela, particularly concerning the PDVSA 2020 8.5 Percent Bond, further delaying the effectiveness of certain authorizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. General Licenses are issued to authorize certain categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs.

Amendments to General Licenses often reflect adjustments in policy or address specific operational challenges faced by businesses and individuals. This particular amendment aims to provide clarity or expand the scope of authorized activities related to Iran.
Such actions are a routine part of OFAC's administration of sanctions programs, ensuring that regulations remain relevant and effective while allowing for legitimate activities.

articles.headline: EU Restricts Trade with 15 Entities Linked to Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union decided on November 25, 2026, to add 15 Russian entities to the list of those subject to tighter export restrictions on dual-use goods and advanced technologies.
These entities are identified as part of Russia's military and industrial complex, with links to or providing support for Russia's defense and security sector.

The decision also included the removal of one entity from the list, as it was determined to have ceased the behavior that led to its listing and provided credible assurances against trading sensitive goods with Russia.

articles.headline: EU Lists 113 Individuals and Entities to Further Restrict Russia's War Financing
body: The European Union imposed additional restrictive measures on 12 individuals and 101 entities on November 16, 2026, for their role in economic sectors that provide substantial revenue to Russia's war of aggression and support its shadow fleet.

The listings include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, aiming to progressively tighten and expand sanctions on Russia's banking sector to cut off financial channels funding the war effort.

The package also cracks down on Russia's e-commerce, including the sole shareholder of Russian retail giant Wildberries and an individual controlling a majority stake in Ozon, another major Russian e-commerce company.

articles.headline: UK Updates Sanctions List with Correction for Russian Ship
body: On November 17, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with a correction related to a specified Russian ship.
The correction is an administrative amendment, clarifying details for the vessel with IMO9958298 and Unique ID RUS3807, which remains subject to shipping sanctions.
These sanctions prohibit the specified ship from entering UK ports, may result in movement or port entry directions, and can lead to detention or refusal of registration on the UK Ship Register.

articles.headline: UK Sanctions List Varied for DPRK Entity Mansudae Overseas Project Group
body: On November 17, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with a variation concerning the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) entity Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies.

A variation signifies a change to a designation following an official decision-making process, which in this case updates information related to Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, also known as Mansudae Art Studio.

This entity has been identified for its involvement in exporting DPRK workers to other nations for construction activities, including the creation of statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the Government of the DPRK or the Workers' Party of Korea.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Updates Sanctions List Entry for DPRK Entity
body: The Security Council 1718 Sanctions Committee updated one entry on its sanctions list on November 16, 2026, pertaining to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).
The updated entry concerns the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, also known as Mansudae Art Studio, located in Pyongyang.

This entity has been previously identified for its role in exporting DPRK workers for construction-related activities, including the creation of statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the Government of the DPRK or the Workers' Party of Korea.

articles.headline: U.S. Economy Grew Faster Than Initially Reported in Q3 2026
body: The U.S. economy experienced a stronger third-quarter growth than initially reported, with the Commerce Department announcing an annualized rate of 4.3%.
This revised figure is a significant jump from the initial estimate of 3.4% and represents the best quarter of economic growth in three years.
Business investment, particularly in software spending driven by major AI-related expenditures, was identified as the primary catalyst for this surge, alongside robust consumer spending.

articles.headline: Stubbornly High Inflation Continues to Impact U.S. Consumers
body: Stubbornly high inflation and its impact on consumers remain a central focus of economic updates this week in the United States.

A key report on inflation is expected to headline a holiday-shortened week, alongside the latest gauge of consumer confidence, which economists anticipate will show continued low confidence due to inflationary pressures.

The U.S. war with Iran, which began in 2026, has fueled inflation throughout the year by curtailing oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz and raising energy prices, subsequently boosting shipping costs for a wide range of goods.

articles.headline: U.S. Intensifies 'Operation Economic Outcast' Against Iran's Shadow Banking Networks
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury has sanctioned over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aiming to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks.

This sweeping effort targets the financial infrastructure underpinning much of Iran's remaining foreign trade, disrupting entities that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions.

According to Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, Iran's shadow banking system is the 'last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,' and Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks.
articles.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury / Middle East Eye

articles.headline: WHO Chief Urges End to U.S. Fuel Blockade on Cuba Amid Healthcare Crisis
body: The head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, has called for the lifting of a U.S. fuel blockade on Cuba, warning that shortages are severely impacting the island's healthcare system and endangering children's lives.
During his visit to Cuba, Tedros announced that the WHO would contribute $2 million to strengthen Cuba's national immunization program and provide essential medical equipment.
The UN has repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, asserting that the decades-long U.S. blockade violates international law and the human rights of all Cubans.

articles.headline: Russia Warns U.S. Against Blockade on Venezuela Amid Sanctions Tightening
body: Russia has warned the United States against 'incautious steps' in tightening sanctions on Venezuela, specifically cautioning against imposing a total blockade on the country.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov urged Washington to assist Venezuelans in bridging existing divides rather than hindering talks between the government and opposition.

These remarks come amidst a visit to Russia by Venezuelan Vice President Delcy Rodriguez, where discussions are expected to include the strengthening of U.S. sanctions and attempts to establish a blockade.

Flagstar Bank, N.A., based in Hicksville, New York, was assessed a civil monetary penalty of $112,000 for a pattern or practice of violating the Flood Disaster Protection Act.

The OCC also announced the termination of a Cease and Desist Order against USAA Federal Savings Bank, Phoenix, Arizona, dated December 18, 2024, indicating the bank has achieved substantial compliance.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for November 2026
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released enforcement actions for November 2026.

articles.headline: BIS Issues Interim Final Rule on Remote Access to Supercomputing Capabilities
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) on November 16, 2026, adding new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors and certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.
The rule addresses concerns about foreign adversaries utilizing chips located in other countries, including through rented cloud infrastructure, to bypass existing export controls.

This IFR also formalizes the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule and establishes a destination-based licensing requirement for exports of advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, with reporting obligations for U.S.-headquartered entities.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities to Entity List for Diversion Risk
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List, effective November 23, 2026.

These entities, located in Malaysia (3), Singapore (3), and Thailand (1), were added due to a significant risk of involvement in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.
For each listed entity, a license is now required for all items subject to the EAR, and license applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: Additions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 7 entities to the Entity List, under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
